Some Results on the Vanishing Conjecture of Differential Operators with Constant CoefficientsThanks: The second named author is supported by the Netherlands Organization of Scientific Research (NWO). The third named author has been partially supported by NSA Grant R1-07-0053

Arno van den Essen, Roel Willems and Wenhua Zhao
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper we prove four cases of the vanishing conjecture of differential operators with constant coefficients and also a conjecture on the Laurent polynomials with no holomorphic parts, which were proposed in [Zh3] by the third named author. We also give two examples to show that the generalizations of both the vanishing conjecture and the Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem [DK] to Laurent formal power series do not hold in general.

Key words and phrases: 
The vanishing conjecture of differential operators with constant coefficients, polytopes of Laurent polynomials, the Jacobian conjecture
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
33C45, 32W99, 14R15

1. Introduction

Let z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{n}) be nn commutative free variables and ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] (resp. ℂ⁡[z−1,z]\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z]) the algebra of polynomials (resp. Laurent polynomials) in zz over ℂ\mathbb{C}. For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, set ∂i:=∂/∂zi\partial_{i}\!:=\partial/\partial z_{i}, and ∂:=(∂1,∂2,…,∂n)\partial\!:=(\partial_{1},\partial_{2},...,\partial_{n}).

We say a differential operator Λ\Lambda of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] is a differential operator with constant coefficients if Λ=h⁡(∂)\Lambda=h(\partial) for some polynomial h⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]h(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi], where ξ=(ξ1,ξ2,…,ξn)\xi=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\dots,\xi_{n}) are another nn commutative variables which also commute with zz. For convenience, we will denote the polynomial h⁡(∂)h(\partial) by Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda(\partial) and simply write Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial).

In this paper, we will prove four cases of the following vanishing conjecture of differential operators with constant coefficients, which was proposed by the third named author in [Zh3].

Conjecture 1.1.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) for some Λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\Lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi]. Assume that Λm​(Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. Then Λm​(Pm+1)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m+1})=0 when m≫0m\gg 0.

Actually, all the cases of the conjecture above that we will prove in this paper also hold in the following more general form.

Conjecture 1.2.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) for some Λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\Lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi]. Assume that Λm​(Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. Then, for any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], we have Λm​(Pm​g)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}g)=0 when m≫0m\gg 0.

Note that, Conjecture 1.1 is just the special case of Conjecture 1.2 with g⁡(z)=P⁡(z)g(z)=P(z). Also, when Λ\Lambda is a homogeneous differential operator of order 22 with constant coefficients, these two conjectures are actually equivalent (See [EZ] and [Zh3]).

Note also that Conjecture 1.2 has recently been generalized by the third named author [Zh4] to the so-called image conjecture of commuting differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients. Actually, Conjecture 1.2 is equivalent to the image conjecture of the commuting differential operators ξi−∂i\xi_{i}-\partial_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) of the polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] for the separable polynomial Λ⁡(ξ)​P​(z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\Lambda(\xi)P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. For more details, see [Zh4].

The main motivation behind Conjecture 1.1 is its connection with the well-known Jacobian conjecture proposed by O. H. Keller [K] in 19391939 (See also [BCW] and [E]). The connection is given by the following theorem proved in [Zh2].

Theorem 1.3.

Let Δn:=∑i=1n∂i2\Delta_{n}\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial_{i}^{2} be the Laplace operator of the polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z]. Then, the Jacobian conjecture holds for all n≥1n\geq 1 iff Conjecture 1.1 with Λ=Δn\Lambda=\Delta_{n} holds for all n≥1n\geq 1.

It has also been shown in [Zh3] that one may replace the Laplace operators Δn\Delta_{n} in the theorem above by any sequence Λn=Λn​(∂)\Lambda_{n}=\Lambda_{n}(\partial) (n≥1)(n\geq 1) of differential operators with Λn​(ξ)\Lambda_{n}(\xi) homogeneous of degree 22 whose ranks go to ∞\infty as n→∞n\to\infty.

The proof of Theorem 1.3 is based on the remarkable symmetric reduction achieved independently by M. de Bondt and the first named author [BE1] and G. Meng [Me]. It also depends on some results obtained in [Zh1] on a deformation of polynomial maps.

Currently, there are only a few cases of Conjecture 1.1 that are known. The best results so far come from M. de Bondt and the first named author’s results [BE2] [BE3] on symmetric polynomial maps via the equivalence obtained by the third named author in [Zh2] and [Zh3]. The results state that Conjecture 1.1 holds for homogeneous quadratic differential operators Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) if either n≤4n\leq 4 (for any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]) or n≤5n\leq 5 with P⁡(z)P(z) homogeneous. The case when Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) is an (integral) power of a homogeneous linear polynomial of ξ\xi is an easy exercise (See also [Zh3]).

In this paper, we will prove four more cases of Conjecture 1.2 and also a conjecture proposed in [Zh3] by the third named author on the Laurent polynomials with no holomorphic parts (See Theorem 5.1).

First, in Section 2, we use a fundamental theorem, Theorem 2.1, in ODE to show that Conjecture 1.2 holds for the one variable case (See Theorem 2.3). Actually, in this case Conjecture 1.2 even holds for all formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) and polynomials g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].

In Section 3, we assume n=2n=2 and show in Theorem 3.1 that Conjecture 1.2 holds for any differential operator Λ\Lambda of the form ∂x−Φ(∂y)\partial_{x}-\Phi(\partial_{y}), where, for convenience, in this section we use (x,y)(x,y) instead of (z1,z2)(z_{1},z_{2}) to denote two free commutative variables and Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) to denote any polynomial in one variable. We also give an example, Example 3.5, to show that the generalizations of both Conjectures 1.1 and 1.2 to formal power series do not hold in general.

In Section 4, we first recall and prove some results on rational polytopes, polytopes with all its vertices having rational coordinates. We then use the remarkable Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem [DK] (See Theorem 4.5) to show what we call the density theorem of polytopes of Laurent polynomials (See Theorem 4.6). We will also show in Lemma 4.9 that Conjecture 1.2 holds when the polytope Poly ​(P)−Poly ​(Λ)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda) has no intersection points with (ℝ≥0)×n({\mathbb{R}}^{\geq 0})^{\times n}. At the end of this section, we give an example, Example 4.11, to show that the Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem can not be generalized to the setting of Laurent formal power series.

In Section 5, we first give a proof for a conjecture proposed in [Zh3] on Laurent polynomials with no holomorphic parts (See Theorem 5.1). We then show in Corollary 5.3 that Conjecture 1.2 holds when either Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) or P⁡(z)P(z) is a monomial of ξ\xi or zz, respectively.

In Section 6, we show in Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.5 that Conjecture 1.2 holds when either Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) or P⁡(z)P(z) is a linear combination of two monomials of ξ\xi or zz, respectively, with different degrees.

2. Proof of the Vanishing Conjecture for One Variable Case

In this section, we consider Conjecture 1.2 for the one-variable case and show that it does hold even for formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) (See Theorem 2.3).

Throughout this section we assume that n=1n=1 and let zz denote a single free variable. For convenience, we also set D:=d/d​zD\!:=d/dz. A different operator Λ=Λ⁡(D)\Lambda=\Lambda(D) is also fixed, where Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) denotes any non-zero polynomial in one variable.

With the notation above, let us first recall the following two well-known fundamental results from ODE (See [L] or any standard text book on ODE).

Theorem 2.1.

Let λi\lambda_{i} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) be the set of all distinct roots of the polynomial Λ⁡(ξ)≠0\Lambda(\xi)\neq 0 with multiplicity mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1. Then, a formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] satisfies the differential equation Λ⁡(D)​P​(z)=0\Lambda(D)P(z)=0 iff P⁡(z)P(z) can be written as a linear combination over ℂ\mathbb{C} of zj​eλi​zz^{j}e^{\lambda_{i}z} (1≤i≤k; 0≤j≤mi−1)(1\leq i\leq k;\,0\leq j\leq m_{i}-1).

Lemma 2.2.

For any distinct λi∈ℂ\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{C} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k), the formal power series {eλi​z| 1≤i≤k}\{e^{\lambda_{i}z}\,|\,1\leq i\leq k\} are linearly independent over the rational function field ℂ⁡(z)\mathbb{C}(z).

In case that a formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) can be written (uniquely) as

(2.1) P⁡(z)=∑i=1kci​(z)​eλi​z\displaystyle P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}(z)e^{\lambda_{i}z}

for some distinct λi∈ℂ\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{C} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) and non-zero ci​(z)∈ℂ​[z]c_{i}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], we call this expression the exponential expansion of P⁡(z)P(z).

The main result of this section is the following theorem.

Theorem 2.3.

For any formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) with Λm​(Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(a)(a) P⁡(z)P(z) must be a polynomial in zz.

(b)(b) Conjecture 1.2 holds for Λ\Lambda, P⁡(z)P(z) and any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].

Proof:  In the proof below, we will freely use the notation fixed above for the differential operator Λ=Λ⁡(D)\Lambda=\Lambda(D) and the polynomial Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi).

Note first that, if P⁡(z)=0P(z)=0, there is nothing to prove. So we assume P⁡(z)≠0P(z)\neq 0.

Since Λ​P=0\Lambda P=0, by Theorem 2.1 and without losing any generality, we may write P⁡(z)P(z) uniquely as in Eq. (2.1) with λi\lambda_{i} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) being distinct roots of Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) and ci​(z)∈ℂ​[z]c_{i}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] with deg⁡ci​(z)≤mi−1\deg c_{i}(z)\leq m_{i}-1 for any 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k.

Assume that P⁡(z)P(z) is not a polynomial. Then, by Lemma 2.2, there exists λi≠0\lambda_{i}\neq 0 for some 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. Identify ℂ\mathbb{C} with ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} and let Σ\Sigma be the polytope or the convex subset in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} generated by λi\lambda_{i} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k). Then, there exists a vertex of Σ\Sigma which is not the origin 0∈ℝ20\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}. Without losing any generality, we assume that λ1\lambda_{1} is such a vertex.

For any m≥1m\geq 1, from Eq. (2.1), it is easy to see that Pm​(z)P^{m}(z) also has an exponential expansion in which em​λ1​ze^{m\lambda_{1}z} appears with the nonzero coefficient cλ1m​(z)c_{\lambda_{1}}^{m}(z).

Since λ1≠0\lambda_{1}\neq 0 and the statement above holds for any m≥1m\geq 1, we see that Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) has infinitely many distinct roots m​λ1m\lambda_{1} (m≥1)(m\geq 1), which is impossible. Therefore, P⁡(z)P(z) must be a polynomial and (a)(a) holds.

To show (b)(b), by (a)(a) and Lemma 2.2, it is easy see that none of non-zero roots of Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) can be involved in Eq. (2.1). Hence we have k=1k=1, λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0 and P​(z)=c1​(z)P(z)=c_{1}(z) with the degree

(2.2) d:=deg⁡P⁡(z)=deg⁡c1​(z)≤m1−1.\displaystyle d\!:=\deg P(z)=\deg c_{1}(z)\leq m_{1}-1.

Since Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) has the root λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0 with multiplicity m1≥1m_{1}\geq 1, we may write Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) as Λ⁡(ξ)=Φ⁡(ξ)​ξm1\Lambda(\xi)=\Phi(\xi)\xi^{m_{1}} for some Φ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\Phi(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi]. Consequently, we have Λ=Λ⁡(D)=Φ⁡(D)​Dm1\Lambda=\Lambda(D)=\Phi(D)D^{m_{1}}.

(2.3) deg⁡Dm​m1​(Pm​g​(z))=(m​d+d′)−m​m1=d′−(m1−d)​m.\displaystyle\deg D^{mm_{1}}(P^{m}g(z))=(md+d^{\prime})-mm_{1}=d^{\prime}-(m_{1}-d)m.

Note that, by Eq. (2.2), we know that m1−d≥1m_{1}-d\geq 1. So, for any m>d′/(m1−d)m>d^{\prime}/(m_{1}-d), we have d′−(m1−d)​m<0d^{\prime}-(m_{1}-d)m<0. Furthermore, by Eq. (2.3), we have, for any m>d′/(m1−d)m>d^{\prime}/(m_{1}-d), Dm​m1​(Pm​g​(z))=0D^{mm_{1}}(P^{m}g(z))=0, hence also

Λm​(Pm​g​(z))=Φm​Dm​m1​(Pm​g​(z))=0.\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}g(z))=\Phi^{m}D^{mm_{1}}(P^{m}g(z))=0.

Therefore, Conjecture 1.2 holds for any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].  □\Box

Two remarks about Theorem 2.3 are as follows.

First, the theorem does not always hold for formal power series g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]. For example, let c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C} such that cc is not a root of Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) and g⁡(z)=ec​zg(z)=e^{cz}. Then, By Theorem 2.3, (a)(a) and Theorem 2.1, it is easy to see that Λm​(Pm​(z)​g​(z))≠0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}(z)g(z))\neq 0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Second, even though the conjecture 1.2 fails for some formal power series g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], by Theorem 2.3, (a)(a), it still holds when g⁡(z)=P⁡(z)g(z)=P(z) without assuming in advance that g⁡(z)=P⁡(z)g(z)=P(z) is a polynomial. In other words, Conjecture 1.1 actually still holds for all formal power series P⁡(z)P(z).

3. Proof of the Vanishing Conjecture for the Differential Operator Λ=∂x−Φ(∂y)\Lambda=\partial_{x}-\Phi(\partial_{y})

Throughout this section, we denote by (x,y)(x,y) instead of (z1,z2)(z_{1},z_{2}) two commutative free variables and by ξ\xi another free variable which commutes with xx and yy. Once and for all, we also fix an arbitrary non-zero polynomial Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) and write it as

(3.1) Φ⁡(ξ)=q0+q1​ξ+⋯+qk​ξk\displaystyle\Phi(\xi)=q_{0}+q_{1}\xi+\cdots+q_{k}\xi^{k}

for some k≥0k\geq 0 and qi∈ℂq_{i}\in\mathbb{C} (0≤i≤k)(0\leq i\leq k).

We will denote by o⁡(Φ⁡(ξ))o(\Phi(\xi)) or o⁡(Φ)o(\Phi) the order of the polynomial Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi), i.e. the least integer m≥0m\geq 0 such that qm≠0q_{m}\neq 0.

In this section, we first give a proof of Conjecture 1.2 for the differential operator Λ=∂x−Φ(∂y)\Lambda=\partial_{x}-\Phi(\partial_{y}) (See the theorem below). We then give an example (See Example 3.5) to show that the generalizations of both Conjectures 1.1 and 1.2 to formal power series P⁡(x,y)∈ℂ⁡[[x,y]]P(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[[x,y]] actually do not hold.

The main result of this section is the following theorem.

Theorem 3.1.

The Conjecture 1.2 holds for the differential operator Λ=∂x−Φ(∂y)\Lambda=\partial_{x}-\Phi(\partial_{y}) and all polynomials P⁡(x,y)∈ℂ⁡[x,y]P(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y].

(3.4) −4​d!​(2​d−r)!(d−r)!​(2​d−2​r)!+(2​d)!(2​d−2​r)!\displaystyle-\,\,\frac{4d!(2d-r)!}{(d-r)!(2d-2r)!}+\frac{(2d)!}{(2d-2r)!} ≥0.\displaystyle\geq 0.

Next we give the following example to show that, for the two variable case, both Conjectures 1.1 and 1.2 fail when P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) is allowed to be a formal power series, instead of just a polynomial.

=(m+1)!​ey≠0.\displaystyle=(m+1)!\,e^{y}\neq 0.

Hence Conjecture 1.1 fails in this case.

Hence, Conjecture 1.2 also fails for the formal power series P⁡(x,y)=x+eyP(x,y)=x+e^{y}.

4. Some Results on Rational Polytopes and the Density Theorem of Polytopes of Laurent Polynomials

In this section, we first recall and prove some results on rational polytopes of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} that will be needed later in this paper. We then use the Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem, Theorem 4.5, to prove what we call the density theorem of polytopes of Laurent polynomials (See Theorem 4.6) along with some of its variations. We will also show in Lemma 4.9 that Conjecture 1.2 holds when the polytope Poly ​(P)−Poly ​(Λ)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda) has no intersection points with (ℝ≥0)×n({\mathbb{R}}^{\geq 0})^{\times n}. Finally, we give an example, Example 4.11, to show that the Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem can not be generalized to the setting of Laurent formal power series.

First, let us fix the following notations and conventions which together with the notations fixed in Section 1 will be used throughout the rest of this paper.

Notation and Convention:

  1. (1)

    We use x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}) to denote the coordinates of the Euclidean space ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. For any u=(a1,a2,…,an)∈ℝnu=(a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, against the traditional notation we set |u|:=∑i=1nai.|u|\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}. Note that |u||u| could be negative for some u∈ℝnu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.

  2. (2)

    For any non-zero u∈ℝnu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, we denote by RuR_{u} the ray with the 0∈ℝn0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} as its (only) end point and passing through uu. When u=0u=0, we let RuR_{u} denote the single point 0∈ℝn0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.

  3. (3)

    For any m∈ℤm\in{\mathbb{Z}}, β∈ℝn\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and a subset A⊂ℝnA\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, we set

    m​A:=\displaystyle mA\!:= {m​u|u∈A},\displaystyle\{mu\,|\,u\in A\},
    β±A:=\displaystyle\beta\pm A\!:= {β±u|u∈A}.\displaystyle\{\beta\pm u\,|\,u\in A\}.
  4. (4)

    We denote by ℝ≥0n{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} the set of the vectors in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} whose components are all non-negative. Furthermore, we introduce a partial order >> for vectors in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} by setting, for any u,v∈ℝnu,v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, u>vu>v if u≠vu\neq v and u−v∈ℝ≥0nu-v\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}; and u≥vu\geq v if u>vu>v or u=vu=v.

  5. (5)

    For any finite subset A={ui| 1≤i≤k}⊂ℝnA=\{u_{i}\,|\,1\leq i\leq k\}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, we set

    (4.1) Poly (A):={∑i=1kciui|ci≥0;∑i=1kci=1}.\displaystyle\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(A)\!:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}u_{i}\,\left.\right|\,c_{i}\geq 0;\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}=1\right\}.

    We call the subset above the polytope generated by the points ui∈ℝnu_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k), or simply, by the subset AA. Throughout the paper, by a polytope we always mean a subset of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} of the form as in Eq. (4.1)(\ref{polytope}).

  6. (6)

    For any u∈ℝnu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, we say uu is a rational point of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} if its all components are rational numbers. We say a polytope is rational if all its vertices are rational.

  7. (7)

    For any fixed Laurent polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z], and any α∈ℤn\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, we denote by [zα]​P​(z)[z^{\alpha}]P(z) the coefficient of zαz^{\alpha} in P⁡(z)P(z). We define the support of P⁡(z)P(z), denoted by Supp ​(P)\text{\rm Supp\,}(P), to be the subset of α∈ℤn\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} such that [zα]​P​(z)≠0[z^{\alpha}]P(z)\neq 0; and the polytope of P⁡(z)P(z), denote by Poly ​(P)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P), to be the polytope generated by Supp ​(P)\text{\rm Supp\,}(P).

  8. (8)

    For any differential operator Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) with Λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\Lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi], we define the support of Λ\Lambda, denoted by Supp ​(Λ)\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda), and the polytope of Λ\Lambda, denoted by Poly ​(Λ)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda), to be the support and the polytope, respectively, of the polynomial Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi).

We start with the following lemma which is well-known (e.g. see [CLO]) and also easy to prove directly. In our later argument we will frequently use this lemma without explicitly referring to it.

Lemma 4.1.

(a)(a) For any polytope Σ\Sigma in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(4.2) m​Σ={∑i=1mui|ui∈Σ}.\displaystyle m\Sigma=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\,|\,u_{i}\in\Sigma\right\}.

(b)(b) For any Laurent polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] and m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(4.3) Poly ​(Pm)=m​Poly ​(P).\displaystyle\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{m})=m\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P).

The following lemma is also well-known. But, for the sake of completeness, we include a proof here.

Lemma 4.2.

For any β∈ℝn\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and any polytope Σ\Sigma in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with Σ∩ℝ≥0n=∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset, there exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that (β+m​Σ)∩ℝ≥0n=∅(\beta+m\Sigma)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset for any m≥Nm\geq N.

Proof:  Assume otherwise, then there exist a strictly increasing sequence {mk|mk∈ℕ}\{m_{k}\,|\,m_{k}\in{\mathbb{N}}\} and a sequence {vk|vk∈(β+mk​Σ)∩ℝ≥0n}\{v_{k}\,|\,v_{k}\in(\beta+m_{k}\Sigma)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\}.

Note that, for any k≥1k\geq 1, we may write vk=β+mk​ukv_{k}=\beta+m_{k}u_{k} for some uk∈Σu_{k}\in\Sigma. Since Σ\Sigma is bounded and closed, and hence compact, the sequence {uk|k≥1}\{u_{k}\,|\,k\geq 1\} has a subsequence which converges to an element u∈Σu\in\Sigma. Without losing any generality, we still denote this subsequence by {uk|k≥1}\{u_{k}\,|\,k\geq 1\}.

Note that, for any k≥1k\geq 1, uk=vk/mk−β/mku_{k}=v_{k}/m_{k}-\beta/m_{k}. Then we have

u=limk→∞uk=limk→∞(vk/mk−β/mk)=limk→∞(vk/mk).\displaystyle u=\lim_{k\to\infty}u_{k}=\lim_{k\to\infty}(v_{k}/m_{k}-\beta/m_{k})=\lim_{k\to\infty}(v_{k}/m_{k}).

Since, for any k≥1k\geq 1, mk≥1m_{k}\geq 1 and vk∈ℝ≥0nv_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}, we have vk/mk∈ℝ≥0nv_{k}/m_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Furthermore, since ℝ≥0n{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} is closed, from the equation above we have u∈ℝ≥0nu\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Therefore, we have u∈Σ∩ℝ≥0nu\in\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}, which is a contradiction. Hence the lemma holds.  □\Box

Lemma 4.3.

For any two rational polytopes Σ\Sigma and Γ\Gamma, we have

(a)(a) If Σ∩Γ≠∅\Sigma\cap\Gamma\neq\emptyset, then it is also a rational polytope.

(b)(b) Σ−Γ:={u−v|u∈Σ,v∈Γ}\Sigma-\Gamma\!:=\{u-v\,|\,u\in\Sigma,\,v\in\Gamma\} is also a rational polytope.

(c)(c) For any rational w∈Σ−Γw\in\Sigma-\Gamma, there exist u∈Σu\in\Sigma and v∈Γv\in\Gamma such that uu, vv are both rational and w=u−vw=u-v.

Proof:  (a)(a) It is well known (e.g. see Theorem 1.1, pp. 29 in [Zi]) that any polytope is a set of common solutions of a system of linear equations or inequalities. It is easy to see that a polytope is rational iff its determining linear equations or inequalities are defined over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, i.e. all the coefficients of unknowns including constant terms of the equations or inequalities are in ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Since Σ∩Γ\Sigma\cap\Gamma is determined by the union of determining linear equations or inequalities of Σ\Sigma and Γ\Gamma, Σ∩Γ\Sigma\cap\Gamma is also a rational polytope if it is not empty.

(b)(b) First, it is easy to see that (−1)​Γ(-1)\Gamma is a rational polytope and Σ−Γ\Sigma-\Gamma is the same as the so-called Minkowski sum of the polytopes Σ\Sigma and Γ\Gamma. It is well known that the Minkowski sum of any two polytopes is also a polytope (e.g. see [CLO] and [Zi]). The reason that the polytope Σ−Γ\Sigma-\Gamma is also rational is because any vertex of Σ−Γ\Sigma-\Gamma is the difference of a vertex of Σ\Sigma and a vertex of Γ\Gamma.

(c)(c) Note that, for the fixed w∈Σ−Γw\in\Sigma-\Gamma in the lemma, the set of elements u∈Σu\in\Sigma such that w=u−vw=u-v for some v∈Γv\in\Gamma is given by Σ∩(w+Γ)\Sigma\cap(w+\Gamma) which is non-empty by the existence of ww itself.

Since both ww and Γ\Gamma are rational, so is w+Γw+\Gamma. By (a)(a) we know that Σ∩(w+Γ)\Sigma\cap(w+\Gamma) is a (non-empty) rational polytope since Σ\Sigma is also rational.

Let uu be any rational point of Σ∩(w+Γ)\Sigma\cap(w+\Gamma), say a vertex of this polytope, and write it as u=w+vu=w+v for some v∈Γv\in\Gamma. Since v=u−wv=u-w, vv is also rational. Hence we get (c)(c).  □\Box

Corollary 4.4.

For any rational polytope Σ\Sigma of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with Σ∩ℝ≥0n≠∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\neq\emptyset, there exists a rational u∈Σ∩ℝ≥0nu\in\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}.

Proof:  Since the rational polytope Σ\Sigma is a closed and bounded subset of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, so is Σ∩ℝ≥0n\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. We may choose an N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} such that Σ∩ℝ≥0n\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} lies inside the polytope generated by 0∈ℝn0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and N​eiNe_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), where eie_{i}’s are the vectors in the standard basis of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. Since the latter polytope is also rational, the corollary follows from Lemma 4.3, (a)(a).  □\Box

Next we prove some results for the polytopes of Laurent polynomials. But, first let us recall the following remarkable theorem which was first conjectured by O. Mathieu [Ma] and later was proved by J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK].

Theorem 4.5.

((Duistermaat and van der Kallen)) For any f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] such that the constant term of fm​(z)f^{m}(z) is equal to zero for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have 0∉Poly ​(f)0\not\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f).

The following result will play some crucial roles in later sections. We believe that it is also important in its own right, so we formulate it as a theorem and call it the density theorem of polytopes of Laurent polynomials.

Theorem 4.6.

((The Density Theorem)) For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] and any rational point u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P), there exists m≥1m\geq 1 such that Ru∩Supp ​(Pm)≠∅R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})\neq\emptyset.

Proof:  Assume otherwise, i.e. Ru∩Supp ​(Pm)=∅R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})=\emptyset for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Since uu is rational, there exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that β:=N​u∈ℤn\beta:=Nu\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}. Hence, we have Ru=RβR_{u}=R_{\beta}. Since u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P) and Poly ​(PN)=N​Poly ​(P)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N})=N\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P), we have

(4.4) β=N​u∈Poly ​(PN).\displaystyle\beta=Nu\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N}).

Let f⁡(z):=z−β​PN​(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\!:=z^{-\beta}P^{N}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z]. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the constant term of fmf^{m} is equal to zero. Otherwise, we would have m​β∈Supp ​(Pm​N)m\beta\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN}) and m​β∈Rβ∩Supp ​(Pm​N)=Ru∩Supp ​(Pm​N)m\beta\in R_{\beta}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN})=R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN}), which contradicts to our assumption on RuR_{u}.

Now apply Theorem 4.5 to f⁡(z)f(z), we have 0∉Poly ​(f)0\not\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f). But, on the other hand, we have

Poly ​(f)=−β+Poly ​(PN).\displaystyle\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)=-\beta+\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N}).

Therefore, β∉Poly ​(PN)\beta\not\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N}) which contradicts to Eq.(4.4). Hence, we have proved the theorem.  □\Box

From the proof above, we can actually get a stronger result.

Corollary 4.7.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] and any rational point u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P), there exist infinitely many mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 such that

Ru∩Supp ​(Pmi)≠∅.\displaystyle R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m_{i}})\neq\emptyset.

Proof:  Assume otherwise, then there exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that Ru∩Supp ​(Pm)=∅R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})=\emptyset for any m≥Nm\geq N.

But, applying Theorem 4.6 to the Laurent polynomial PN​(z)P^{N}(z) and the rational point N​u∈Poly ​(PN)Nu\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N}), we see that there exists m≥1m\geq 1, such that

∅≠RN​u∩Supp ​(Pm​N)=Ru∩Supp ​(Pm​N).\displaystyle\emptyset\neq R_{Nu}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN})=R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN}).

Since m​N≥NmN\geq N, we get a contradiction.  □\Box

When P⁡(z)P(z) is homogeneous with respect to the generalized degree (counting deg⁡zi−1=−1\deg z_{i}^{-1}=-1 for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n) of Laurent polynomials, we have the following more precise result.

Corollary 4.8.

For any homogeneous Laurent polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≠0d\neq 0, and any rational point u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P), there exist infinitely many mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 such that mi​u∈Supp ​(Pmi)m_{i}u\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m_{i}}).

Proof:  First, since deg⁡P=d\deg P=d, we see that Poly ​(P)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P) lies in the affine hyperplane HH determined by the equation ∑i=1nxi=d\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=d. Since u∈Poly ​(P)⊂Hu\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)\subset H, we have |u|=d|u|=d.

Second, by Corollary 4.7, we know that there exist infinitely many mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 such that Ru∩Supp ​(Pmi)≠∅R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m_{i}})\neq\emptyset. We fix any such an mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 and choose any βi∈Ru∩Supp ​(Pmi)\beta_{i}\in R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m_{i}}) (Actually, such βi\beta_{i} is unique as the intersection point of RuR_{u} with the affine hyperplane mi​Hm_{i}H). Write βi=ki​u\beta_{i}=k_{i}u for some ki≥0k_{i}\geq 0. Then we have |βi|=ki​|u|=ki​d|\beta_{i}|=k_{i}|u|=k_{i}d. Since βi∈Supp ​(Pmi)⊂mi​Poly ​(P)⊂mi​H\beta_{i}\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m_{i}})\subset m_{i}\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)\subset m_{i}H, we have |βi|=mi​d|\beta_{i}|=m_{i}d. Hence we have ki=mik_{i}=m_{i} and βi=mi​u\beta_{i}=m_{i}u.  □\Box

Next we prove the following general result on Conjecture 1.2, which will be needed in Section 6.

Lemma 4.9.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) any differential operator with constant coefficients. Assume

(4.5) (Poly ​(P)−Poly ​(Λ))∩ℝ≥0n=∅.\displaystyle(\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda))\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset.

Then, we have

(a)(a) for any m≥1m\geq 1, Λm​(Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=0.

(b)(b) for any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], Λm​(Pm​g)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}g)=0 when m≫0m\gg 0.

Proof:  We first prove (b)(b) as follows.

First, note that, by the linearity of Λm​(Pm​g)\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}g) (m≥1)(m\geq 1) on g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], it is easy to see that we may assume g⁡(z)=zγg(z)=z^{\gamma} for some γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Second, let Σ:=Poly ​(P)−Poly ​(Λ)\Sigma\!:=\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda). Then, we have that Σ∩ℝ≥0n=∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset and also, by Lemma 4.3, (b)(b), Σ\Sigma is a polytope of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.

Apply Lemma 4.2 to the polytope Σ\Sigma and γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we get a N≥1N\geq 1 such that, for any m≥Nm\geq N,

(4.6) (γ+m​Σ)∩ℝ≥0n=∅.\displaystyle(\gamma+m\Sigma)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset.

On the other hand, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(4.7) m​Σ=m​Poly ​(P)−m​Poly ​(Λ)=Poly ​(Pm)−Poly ​(Λm).\displaystyle m\Sigma=m\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-m\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda)=\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{m})-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda^{m}).

Therefore, by Eq.(4.6) and the equation above, we have

(4.8) ℝ≥0n∩(γ+(Poly ​(Pm)−Poly ​(Λm))=∅CLOSE\displaystyle{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\cap\left(\gamma+(\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{m})-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda^{m})\right)=\emptyset

for any m≥Nm\geq N.

Consequently, for any m≥Nm\geq N, λ∈Supp ​(Pm)⊂Poly ​(Pm)\lambda\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})\subset\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{m}) and μ∈Supp ​(Λm)⊂Poly ​(Λm)\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m})\subset\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda^{m}), we have

(4.9) (γ+λ)−μ=γ+(λ−μ)∉ℝ≥0n.\displaystyle(\gamma+\lambda)-\mu=\gamma+(\lambda-\mu)\not\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}.

Hence, we have ∂μzγ+λ=0\partial^{\mu}z^{\gamma+\lambda}=0. Since Λm\Lambda^{m} is a linear combination of ∂μ\partial^{\mu} (μ∈Supp ​(Λm))(\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m})) and zγ​Pm​(z)z^{\gamma}P^{m}(z) is a linear combination over ℂ\mathbb{C} of zγ+λz^{\gamma+\lambda} (λ∈Supp ​(Pm))(\lambda\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})), we have Λm​(zγ​Pm​(z))=0\Lambda^{m}(z^{\gamma}P^{m}(z))=0 for any m≥Nm\geq N. Therefore, we have proved (b)(b).

To see (a)(a) also holds, note that, by choosing γ=0∈ℕn\gamma=0\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} in the proof above, Eq.(4.6) actually holds for any m≥1m\geq 1. This is because the condition Σ∩ℝ≥0n=∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset implies directly m​Σ∩ℝ≥0n=∅m\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset for any m≥1m\geq 1. Therefore, the argument above also goes through with N=1N=1 and γ=0\gamma=0, which means (a)(a) also holds.  □\Box

Remark 4.10.

Note that, by Lemma 4.9, (a)(a), we see that the condition given in Eq. (4.5)(\ref{Pnot>L-e1}) implies the condition in Conjecture 1.2. By Lemma 4.9, (b)(b), we see that Conjecture 1.2 does hold in this case.

Finally, let us point out that, like Conjectures 1.1 and 1.2, the Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem, Theorem 4.5 can not be generalized to Laurent formal power series either.

Example 4.11.

Let f⁡(x,y)=y−1​(1+x−1​ey)f(x,y)=y^{-1}(1+x^{-1}e^{y}) and g⁡(x,y)=xg(x,y)=x. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, it is easy to check that, the constant term of fmf^{m} is equal to zero, but the constant term of fm​gf^{m}g is equal to 1/(m−1)!≠01/(m-1)!\neq 0. Therefore, 0∈Supp ​(fm​g)0\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m}g) for each m≥1m\geq 1.

Assume that the statement of Theorem 4.5 holds for f⁡(x,y)f(x,y), i.e. 0∉Poly ​(f)0\not\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f), then, as shown in [DK], we will have 0∉Supp ​(fm​g)0\not\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m}g) when m≫0m\gg 0. But this contradicts to the fact pointed out above, i.e. 0∈Supp ​(fm​g)0\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m}g) for each m≥1m\geq 1. Hence the statement of Theorem 4.5 fails for the Laurent power series f⁡(x,y)f(x,y).

5. A Theorem on Laurent Polynomials with no Holomorphic Parts and the Vanishing Conjecture when Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda(\partial) or P⁡(z)P(z) is a Monomial

In this section, we first prove a conjecture proposed in [Zh3] on Laurent polynomials with no holomorphic parts (See Theorem 5.1). By using this result, we then show in Corollary 5.3 that Conjecture 1.2 holds when the polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) or the differential operators Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) is a monomial of zz or ∂\partial, respectively.

Theorem 5.1.

Let f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] such that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the holomorphic part of fmf^{m} is equal to zero, i.e. Supp ​(fm)∩ℝ≥0n=∅\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m})\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset, or equivalently, [zα]​fm=0[z^{\alpha}]f^{m}=0 for any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. Then, for any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z], the holomorphic part of g​fmgf^{m} is equal to zero when m≫0m\gg 0.

Proof:  Since the subset of Laurent polynomials with no holomorphic parts is a subspace of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z], and g⁡(z)g(z) is a linear combination over ℂ\mathbb{C} of finitely many monomials of zz, it is easy to see that we may assume g⁡(z)=zβg(z)=z^{\beta} for some β∈ℤn\beta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}.

Let us first show Poly ​(f)∩ℝ≥0n=∅\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset by the contradiction method.

Assume otherwise, i.e. Poly ​(f)∩ℝ≥0n≠∅\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\neq\emptyset. Since Poly ​(f)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f) is a rational polytope, by Corollary 4.4, there exists a rational u∈Poly ​(f)∩ℝ≥0nu\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Below we fix any such a rational point uu.

Apply Theorem 4.6 to f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z] and the rational point u∈Poly ​(f)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f), there exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that Ru∩Supp ​(fN)≠∅R_{u}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{N})\neq\emptyset. Note that Ru⊂ℝ≥0nR_{u}\subset{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} since u∈ℝ≥0nu\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. So we have ℝ≥0n∩Supp ​(fN)≠∅{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{N})\neq\emptyset, and hence the holomorphic part of fNf^{N} is not zero, which is a contradiction. Therefore, we must have Poly ​(f)∩ℝ≥0n=∅\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset.

Next, apply Lemma 4.2 to the polytope Poly ​(f)\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f) and β∈ℕn\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we know that ℝ≥0n∩(β+m​Poly ​(f))=∅{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\cap(\beta+m\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f))=\emptyset when m≫0m\gg 0. Since, for any m≥1m\geq 1, m​Poly ​(f)=Poly ​(fm)m\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f)=\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f^{m}) and Supp ​(fm)⊂Poly ​(fm)\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m})\subset\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(f^{m}), we have ℝ≥0n∩(β+Supp ​(fm))=∅{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\cap(\beta+\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m}))=\emptyset when m≫0m\gg 0.

On the other hand, it is easy to see that Supp ​(zβ​fm)=β+Supp ​(fm)\text{\rm Supp\,}(z^{\beta}f^{m})=\beta+\text{\rm Supp\,}(f^{m}) for any m≥1m\geq 1. Therefore, we have ℝ≥0n∩Supp ​(zβ​fm)=∅{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\cap\text{\rm Supp\,}(z^{\beta}f^{m})=\emptyset when m≫0m\gg 0, which means that the theorem holds for g⁡(z)=zβg(z)=z^{\beta}.  □\Box

Next, we use Theorem 5.1 to show that Conjecture 1.2 holds when P⁡(z)P(z) or Λ\Lambda is a monomial of zz or ∂\partial, respectively. But, first, let us formulate the following simple observation as a lemma since it will be crucial for our later arguments.

Lemma 5.2.

For any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have that, ∂αzβ=0\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta}=0 iff β≱α\beta\not\geq\alpha, or equivalently, β−α∉ℝ≥0n\beta-\alpha\not\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}.

Note that the lemma above is not necessarily true for β∈ℤn\ℕn\beta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}\backslash{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Corollary 5.3.

Conjecture 1.2 holds if either Λ=∂α\Lambda=\partial^{\alpha} or P⁡(z)=zαP(z)=z^{\alpha} for some α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Proof:  We prove the corollary for the case that P⁡(z)=zαP(z)=z^{\alpha} for some α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. The proof for the other case is similar.

First, by the linearity on g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], we may assume that g⁡(z)=zγg(z)=z^{\gamma} for some γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Second, for any h⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]h(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi] and any β∈ℕn\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, by Lemma 5.2, it is easy to see that we have the following equivalences:

(5.1) h⁡(∂)​zβ=0\displaystyle h(\partial)z^{\beta}=0\quad ⇔β≱μ for any μ∈Supp (h)\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\quad\beta\not\geq\mu\mbox{ for any }\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(h)
⇔Supp (zβh(z−1))∩ℝ≥0n=∅.\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\quad\text{\rm Supp\,}(z^{\beta}h(z^{-1}))\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset.

Note that the last statement above is equivalent to saying that the holomorphic part of the Laurent polynomial zβ​h​(z−1)z^{\beta}h(z^{-1}) is equal to zero.

Now, we write Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) for some polynomial Λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\Lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi] and set f⁡(z):=Λ⁡(z−1)​zαf(z)\!:=\Lambda(z^{-1})z^{\alpha}. Since Λm​(Pm)=Λm​(zm​α)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=\Lambda^{m}(z^{m\alpha})=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1, applying the equivalences in Eq. (5.1) with h​(ξ)=Λm​(ξ)h(\xi)=\Lambda^{m}(\xi) and β=m​α\beta=m\alpha, we know that the holomorphic part of fm=Λm​(z−1)​zm​αf^{m}=\Lambda^{m}(z^{-1})z^{m\alpha} is equal to zero for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Applying Theorem 5.1 to f⁡(z)f(z) and g⁡(z)=zγg(z)=z^{\gamma}, we know that there exists a N≥1N\geq 1 such that the holomorphic part of fm​zγ=Λm​(z−1)​zm​α+γf^{m}z^{\gamma}=\Lambda^{m}(z^{-1})z^{m\alpha+\gamma} is equal to zero for any m≥Nm\geq N. For any fixed m≥Nm\geq N, applying the equivalences in Eq. (5.1) with h​(ξ)=Λm​(ξ)h(\xi)=\Lambda^{m}(\xi) and β=m​α+γ\beta=m\alpha+\gamma, we get Λm​(Pm​zγ)=Λm​(zm​α+γ)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m}z^{\gamma})=\Lambda^{m}(z^{m\alpha+\gamma})=0. Therefore, Conjecture 1.2 does hold in this case.  □\Box

6. Proof of the Vanishing Conjecture for the Differential Operator Λ=a∂α+b∂β\Lambda=a\partial^{\alpha}+b\partial^{\beta} with |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta|

In this section, we prove the following case of Conjecture 1.2.

Theorem 6.1.

Let α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta|, and Λ=a∂α+b∂β\Lambda=a\partial^{\alpha}+b\partial^{\beta} for some a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mathbb{C}. Then, Conjecture 1.2 holds for the differential operator Λ\Lambda and any homogeneous P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].

First, let us consider the following simple cases of the theorem above.

If a=b=0a=b=0, then Λ=0\Lambda=0. There is nothing to prove. If only one of the aa and bb is zero, then, after a change of variables, we may assume Λ=∂γ\Lambda=\partial^{\gamma} for some γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. Then Conjecture 1.2 in this case follows directly from Corollary 5.3.

Therefore we may assume that aa and bb are both nonzero. Then, by using the fact that α≠β\alpha\neq\beta, it is easy to see that, after a change of variables, we may assume a=b≠0a=b\neq 0. Note also that in general Conjecture 1.2 holds for a differential operator iff it holds for any nonzero scalar multiple of the differential operator. So we may further assume that a=b=1a=b=1. Therefore, we can reduce Theorem 6.1 to the case when Λ=∂α+∂β\Lambda=\partial^{\alpha}+\partial^{\beta} for some α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta|.

Throughout the rest of this section, we will fix a differential operator Λ\Lambda as above and a homogeneous polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] of degree d=deg⁡P≥0d=\deg P\geq 0 such that Λm​(Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. We divide the proof of Theorem 6.1 for this case into several lemmas.

Lemma 6.2.

(a)(a) For any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(6.1) Supp (Λm)={kα+ℓβ|k,ℓ∈ℕ;k+ℓ=m}.\displaystyle\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m})=\{k\alpha+\ell\beta\,|\,k,\ell\in{\mathbb{N}};k+\ell=m\}.

(b)(b) For any m,k≥1m,k\geq 1 and u∈Supp ​(Λk)u\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{k}), m​u∈Supp ​(Λm​k)mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{mk}).

Proof:  (a)(a) The statement follows directly from the binomial expansion of Λm=(∂α+∂β)m\Lambda^{m}=(\partial^{\alpha}+\partial^{\beta})^{m}.

(b)(b) By (a)(a), we may write u=r​α+s​βu=r\alpha+s\beta for some r,s∈ℕr,s\in{\mathbb{N}} with r+s=kr+s=k. Then, we have m​u=m​r​α+m​s​βmu=mr\alpha+ms\beta. Since m​r,m​s∈ℕmr,ms\in{\mathbb{N}} and m​r+m​s=m​kmr+ms=mk, by (a)(a) again we have m​u∈Supp ​(Λm​k)mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{mk}).  □\Box

Lemma 6.3.

For any fixed m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(a)(a) ∂μPm=0\partial^{\mu}P^{m}=0 for any μ∈Supp ​(Λm)\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m}).

(b)(b) for any μ∈Supp ​(Λm)\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m}) and γ∈Supp ​(Pm)\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m}), we have γ≱μ\gamma\not\geq\mu or equivalently, γ−μ∉ℝ≥0n\gamma-\mu\not\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}.

Proof:  (a)(a) We first consider

(6.2) 0\displaystyle 0 =Λm(Pm)=(∂α+∂β)m(Pm)=∑k,ℓ≥0k+ℓ=m(mk)∂k​α+ℓ​β(Pm).\displaystyle=\Lambda^{m}(P^{m})=(\partial^{\alpha}+\partial^{\beta})^{m}(P^{m})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\geq 0\\ k+\ell=m\end{subarray}}\binom{m}{k}\partial^{k\alpha+\ell\beta}(P^{m}).

Note that, for any k,ℓ≥0k,\ell\geq 0 with k+ℓ=mk+\ell=m, we have

(6.3) deg⁡(∂k​α+ℓ​βPm)=m​d−(k​|α|+ℓ​|β|).\displaystyle\deg(\partial^{k\alpha+\ell\beta}P^{m})=md-(k|\alpha|+\ell|\beta|).

Assume that, for some k′,ℓ′∈ℕnk^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with k′+ℓ′=mk^{\prime}+\ell^{\prime}=m, we have

deg⁡(∂k′​α+ℓ′​βPm)=deg⁡(∂k​α+ℓ​βPm)\displaystyle\deg(\partial^{k^{\prime}\alpha+\ell^{\prime}\beta}P^{m})=\deg(\partial^{k\alpha+\ell\beta}P^{m})

Then, by Eq. (6.3), we get

k​|α|+ℓ​|β|\displaystyle k|\alpha|+\ell|\beta| =k′​|α|+ℓ′​|β|,\displaystyle=k^{\prime}|\alpha|+\ell^{\prime}|\beta|,
(6.4) (k−k′)​|α|\displaystyle(k-k^{\prime})|\alpha| =(ℓ′−ℓ)​|β|.\displaystyle=(\ell^{\prime}-\ell)|\beta|.

Since k+ℓ=k′+ℓ′=mk+\ell=k^{\prime}+\ell^{\prime}=m, we have k−k′=ℓ′−ℓk-k^{\prime}=\ell^{\prime}-\ell. Combining Eq. (6.4) with the fact that |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta|, we see that k−k′=ℓ′−ℓ=0k-k^{\prime}=\ell^{\prime}-\ell=0. Therefore, all the terms in the sum of Eq. (6.2) have different degrees. Hence they all have to be zero.

On the other hand, by Lemma 6.2, (a)(a), any μ∈Supp ​(Λm)\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m}) has the form k​α+ℓ​βk\alpha+\ell\beta for some k,l∈ℕk,l\in{\mathbb{N}} with k+l=mk+l=m. Hence (a)(a) follows.

(b)(b) First, we write Pm​(z)P^{m}(z) as Pm​(z)=∑γ∈Supp ​(Pm)bγ​zγP^{m}(z)=\sum_{\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})}b_{\gamma}z^{\gamma} with bγ∈ℂ×b_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}. For any μ∈Supp ​(Λm)\mu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{m}), by (a)(a) and also Lemma 5.2, we have

(6.5) 0=∂μ(Pm)=∑γ∈Supp ​(Pm)bγ​∂μ(zγ)=∑γ∈Supp ​(Pm)γ≥μbγ​zγ−μ.\displaystyle 0=\partial^{\mu}(P^{m})=\sum_{\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})}b_{\gamma}\partial^{\mu}(z^{\gamma})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m})\\ \gamma\geq\mu\end{subarray}}b_{\gamma}z^{\gamma-\mu}.

Note that bγ≠0b_{\gamma}\neq 0 for any γ∈Supp ​(Pm)\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m}) and, for any γ1≠γ2∈Supp ​(Pm)\gamma_{1}\neq\gamma_{2}\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m}), zγ1−μ≠zγ2−μz^{\gamma_{1}-\mu}\neq z^{\gamma_{2}-\mu}. Then, from Eq. (6.5) we see that there can not be any γ∈Supp ​(Pm)\gamma\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{m}) such that γ≥μ\gamma\geq\mu. Hence (b)(b) also holds.  □\Box

Lemma 6.4.

Let u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P) and v∈Poly ​(Λ)v\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda). Assume that both uu and vv are rational. Then, we have, u≱vu\not\geq v.

Proof:  First, denote by Lα,βL_{\alpha,\beta} the line segment in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} connecting α\alpha and β\beta. Then it is easy to see that Poly ​(Λ)=Lα,β\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda)=L_{\alpha,\beta}. Since both α\alpha and β\beta are rational, it is easy to check that, a point of Lα,βL_{\alpha,\beta} is rational iff it is a linear combination of α\alpha and β\beta with rational coefficients. Therefore, we may write v=r​α+s​βv=r\alpha+s\beta for some rational r,s≥0r,s\geq 0 with r+s=1r+s=1. Let N≥1N\geq 1 such that N​r,N​s∈ℕNr,Ns\in{\mathbb{N}}. Since N​r+N​s=NNr+Ns=N, by Lemma 6.2, (a)(a), we have N​v=N​r​α+N​s​β∈Supp ​(ΛN)Nv=Nr\alpha+Ns\beta\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{N}).

Second, apply Corollary 4.8 to the homogeneous polynomial PNP^{N} and the rational point N​u∈Poly ​(PN)Nu\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P^{N}), there exists m≥1m\geq 1 such that m​N​u∈Supp ​(Pm​N)mNu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN}). Since N​v∈Supp ​(ΛN)Nv\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{N}), by Lemma 6.2, (b)(b), we have m​N​v∈Supp ​(Λm​N)mNv\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{mN}).

Note that m​N​u∈Supp ​(Pm​N)mNu\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(P^{mN}) and m​N​v∈Supp ​(Λm​N)mNv\in\text{\rm Supp\,}(\Lambda^{mN}) are both rational, by Lemma 6.3, (b)(b), we have m​N​u−m​N​v=m​N​(u−v)∉ℝ≥0nmNu-mNv=mN(u-v)\not\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Since m​N>0mN>0, we also have (u−v)∉ℝ≥0n(u-v)\not\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}, i.e. u≱vu\not\geq v.  □\Box

Now, we can prove the main result, Theorem 6.1, of this section as follows.

Proof of Theorem 6.1: First, by the reductions given at the beginning of this section, we may assume that the differential operator Λ=∂α+∂β\Lambda=\partial^{\alpha}+\partial^{\beta} for some α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta|.

Second, let Σ:=Poly ​(P)−Poly ​(Λ)\Sigma\!:=\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P)-\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda). Then, by Lemma 4.9, it will be enough to show that Σ∩ℝ≥0n=∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}=\emptyset.

We assume otherwise, i.e. Σ∩ℝ≥0n≠∅\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\neq\emptyset, and derive a contradiction as follows.

Note first that, by Lemma 4.3, (b)(b), we know that Σ\Sigma is a rational polytope. By Corollary 4.4, there exists a rational point w∈Σ∩ℝ≥0nw\in\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Then, by lemma 4.3, (c)(c), there exist u∈Poly ​(P)u\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(P) and v∈Poly ​(Λ)v\in\mbox{\rm Poly\,}(\Lambda) such that uu, vv are both rational and u−v=w∈Σ∩ℝ≥0n⊂ℝ≥0nu-v=w\in\Sigma\cap{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\subset{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. But this contradicts to Lemma 6.4. Hence we have proved the theorem. □\Box

Finally, let us point out that, by similar arguments as in the proof of Theorem 6.1, it is easy to see that Conjecture 1.2 also holds for the following case.

Corollary 6.5.

Let α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with |α|≠|β||\alpha|\neq|\beta| and P⁡(z)=a​zα+b​zβP(z)=az^{\alpha}+bz^{\beta} for some a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mathbb{C}. Let Λ=Λ⁡(∂)\Lambda=\Lambda(\partial) with Λ⁡(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) homogeneous. Then Conjecture 1.2 holds for Λ\Lambda, P⁡(z)P(z) and any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].
